name: Khaman Dhokla
cuisine: Gujarati (instant besan khaman, the everyday farsan of Gujarati homes and Mumbai farsan shops)

ingredients.name: Green chilli (hari mirch), for the paste

equipment: A small flat-bottomed steel plate (5–6 inch), small tiffin box, or wide katori, to steam the batter in
Mixing bowl and whisk (a fork works; a balloon whisk gives a smoother batter)
Small tadka pan (or the smallest kadai you have) for the tempering
Knife, and a toothpick or thin skewer for the doneness test
Measuring spoons; a small grater for the ginger (or crush ginger and chilli in a mortar and pestle)
A thick cloth or tongs to lift the hot plate out of the steamer

steps.title: Heat the steamer water
steps.text: Pour about 3 cm (about 2 cups) water into the steamer or cooker and set it on medium-high heat with the stand inside and the lid on.
steps.tip: The steamer must be at a full rolling boil before the batter goes in; batter that sits waiting after the eno goes flat.
steps.visualCue: Water level below the top of the stand.
steps.cameraCheck: The steamer with the stand and water inside
steps.videoShot: Water pouring into a cooker with a steel stand in it.

steps.title: Grease the plate
steps.text: Smear a few drops of oil over the base and sides of a 5–6 inch steel plate or tiffin box.
steps.visualCue: A thin, even shine; no pools of oil.
steps.videoShot: A fingertip spreading oil over a small steel plate.

steps.title: Make the ginger-chilli paste
steps.text: Grate 2 g (½ tsp) ginger and crush ½ small green chilli (2 g) into a paste.
steps.visualCue: A coarse, wet, pale-green paste.
steps.videoShot: Ginger and chilli being crushed in a small mortar.

steps.title: Sift the besan
steps.text: Sift 40 g (about ⅓ cup) besan into the mixing bowl.
steps.tip: Lumpy or old besan gives dense khaman; sifting lets in air and catches lumps.
steps.visualCue: A soft, lump-free mound of yellow flour.
steps.videoShot: Besan falling through a sieve into a bowl.

steps.title: Add sooji, sugar and salt
steps.text: Add 1 level tsp sooji, ¾ tsp sugar and a scant ¼ tsp salt. Add a tiny pinch of turmeric if you want a deeper yellow.
steps.tip: Keep turmeric tiny or skip it; eno reacts with turmeric and can leave red spots.
steps.visualCue: White specks of sooji and sugar on the besan.
steps.cameraCheck: The dry mix in the bowl
steps.videoShot: Spoons tipping sooji, sugar and salt onto the besan.

steps.title: Add the paste, lemon and oil
steps.text: Add the ginger-chilli paste, 1½ tsp lemon juice and ½ tsp oil.
steps.visualCue: Wet patches on the flour.
steps.cameraCheck: The bowl with the wet ingredients on top
steps.videoShot: Lemon juice squeezed over the flour.

steps.title: Add water and whisk
steps.text: Pour in 45 ml (3 tbsp) water and whisk in one direction until completely smooth.
steps.tip: Too thick (stays in a heap)? Add 1 tsp water. Too thin (runs like milk)? Add 1 tsp besan.
steps.visualCue: A smooth, thick but pourable batter, like idli batter, with no lumps; it falls from the whisk in a thick ribbon.
steps.videoShot: A whisk lifting and dropping a ribbon of yellow batter.

steps.title: Rest the batter
steps.text: Cover and leave for 10 min so the sooji softens.
steps.visualCue: The batter has thickened slightly.
steps.videoShot: A plate covering the bowl.

steps.title: Check the steamer
steps.text: Make sure the water is at a rolling boil and steam is escaping.
steps.visualCue: Strong steam when you lift the lid.
steps.cameraCheck: Steam coming out of the open steamer
steps.videoShot: The lid lifting off in a puff of steam.

steps.title: Stir the batter once more
steps.text: Whisk the rested batter for 10 sec. If it has become stiff, add 1 tsp water.
steps.visualCue: Smooth, ribbon-like again.
steps.videoShot: A quick whisk of the batter.

steps.title: Measure the eno
steps.text: Measure a scant ½ tsp (2 g) plain eno into a dry spoon and keep it next to the bowl.
steps.visualCue: A small heap of white powder.
steps.videoShot: Eno tipped from a sachet onto a spoon.

steps.title: Add the eno and a splash of water
steps.text: Tip the eno onto the batter and pour 1 tsp water directly on top of it.
steps.visualCue: The eno fizzes and bubbles at once.
steps.cameraCheck: The fizzing spot on the batter
steps.videoShot: Water hitting the eno and making it foam.

steps.title: Fold quickly
steps.text: Stir in one direction for 5–8 sec only, until the eno is just mixed in.
steps.tip: Do not beat after the eno goes in; you knock out the bubbles.
steps.visualCue: The batter turns pale, frothy and almost doubles in volume.
steps.cameraCheck: The foamy batter in the bowl
steps.videoShot: A spoon folding light, airy batter.

steps.title: Pour into the plate
steps.text: Pour the batter at once into the greased plate and tap it gently on the counter once.
steps.visualCue: An even layer about 2–2.5 cm deep.
steps.videoShot: Frothy batter pouring into the steel plate.

steps.title: Steam
steps.text: Place the plate on the stand, cover, and steam on medium-high heat for 12 min. Do not open the lid for the first 10 min.
steps.tip: In a cooker, take the whistle off; the weight would build pressure and dry the khaman.
steps.visualCue: (Check in step 16.)
steps.cameraCheck: The closed steamer on the flame
steps.videoShot: Steam escaping round the edge of a closed lid.

steps.title: Test with a toothpick
steps.text: Open the lid, push a toothpick into the centre and pull it out.
steps.visualCue: The toothpick comes out clean; the top is risen, spongy and springs back when pressed. If batter clings, steam 2 min more.
steps.cameraCheck: The clean toothpick next to the khaman
steps.videoShot: A toothpick sliding out of the yellow sponge.

steps.title: Cool slightly
steps.text: Lift the plate out with a cloth and leave it for 5 min.
steps.visualCue: Stops steaming heavily; the edges pull away a little.
steps.cameraCheck: The plate out of the steamer
steps.videoShot: The khaman sitting on the counter with light steam.

steps.title: Heat the tempering oil
steps.text: Heat 1 tsp oil in the tadka pan on medium heat.
steps.visualCue: The oil shimmers.
steps.videoShot: Oil spreading across a small pan.

steps.title: Crackle the mustard
steps.text: Add ¼ tsp mustard seeds and wait for them to pop.
steps.visualCue: The seeds pop and jump; a nutty smell.
steps.videoShot: Mustard seeds crackling in hot oil.

steps.title: Add sesame, hing, curry leaves and chilli
steps.text: Lower the heat and add ½ tsp sesame seeds, a tiny pinch of hing, 5–6 curry leaves and 1 slit green chilli.
steps.tip: Curry leaves spit; drop them in from a little height and stand back.
steps.visualCue: Sesame turns pale gold, curry leaves crisp up and turn bright green.
steps.videoShot: Curry leaves spluttering into the oil.

steps.title: Add water and sugar
steps.text: Take the pan off the heat, add 35 ml water carefully (it splutters), then 1¼ tsp sugar. Put it back on the heat and bring it to a boil.
steps.visualCue: The sugar has dissolved and the liquid is bubbling.
steps.videoShot: Water hissing into the tempering, then sugar stirring in.

steps.title: Cut the khaman
steps.text: Cut the khaman into 6 squares (or diamonds) while still in the plate.
steps.visualCue: Clean cuts showing an open, spongy, honeycomb inside.
steps.videoShot: A knife cutting squares through the yellow sponge.

steps.title: Pour the tempering
steps.text: Spoon the hot tempering water evenly over all the pieces, including the cuts.
steps.visualCue: The khaman soaks it up and turns glossy; the mustard and curry leaves sit on top.
steps.videoShot: A spoon drizzling the shiny tempering over the squares.

steps.title: Rest to soak
steps.text: Leave for 5 min so the liquid is absorbed.
steps.visualCue: No pool of liquid left in the plate; the pieces are moist and soft.
steps.videoShot: Close-up of a moist, spongy piece.

steps.title: Garnish and serve
steps.text: Sprinkle 1 tbsp chopped coriander and 1 tbsp grated coconut on top and serve with green chutney.
steps.visualCue: Bright yellow squares with green, white and black flecks.
steps.videoShot: Coriander and coconut falling onto the khaman, then a piece dipped in chutney.

reasons: steamed, not fried, made from pulse flour, so it gives about 10 g protein, 6 g fibre and a lot of folate and magnesium for about 300 kcal, with only about 1¾ tsp oil and no saturated-fat-heavy ghee. Against it: 8 g added sugar in the tempering, and about 765 mg sodium (eno adds nearly as much sodium as the salt), with few vegetables. Farsan-shop khaman is usually sweeter, oilier and served with sweet chutney and sometimes sev or fried chillies.

researchRating.basis: one of India's best-known Gujarati snacks, with very popular recipes (Archana's Kitchen instant khaman dhokla shows 11,298 ratings; Hebbar's Kitchen nylon khaman 5/5 from 58 votes) and whole Mumbai shops built around it (Radhe Dhokla, KK Dhokla, Rajubhai Dhoklawala, Jain and Gujarati farsan marts). Small deduction because many home cooks report flat or dense results at first and the sweetness divides opinion outside Gujarat.

storage: Best the same day; it dries out and firms up in the fridge. Fridge: up to 2 days in an airtight box, within 2 hours of making. Freezer: not recommended (the sponge turns crumbly and wet when thawed). To revive, sprinkle 1–2 tsp water, cover and steam for 2–3 min, or microwave covered for 20–30 sec.
leftoverRemix: Sev khamani-style crumble. Crumble 2–3 leftover pieces with your fingers, toss them in a pan with ½ tsp oil, a pinch of mustard seeds, a little crushed green chilli, a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of sugar for 1–2 min, then top with chopped coriander, pomegranate seeds and a spoon of nylon sev: day-old khaman turned into the crumbly, tangy Surti farsan.
burnOff: about 4.3 km of running (300 ÷ 70 kcal/km, for a 70 kg adult), or about 6 km of brisk walking (about 1 h 12 min at 5 km/h, using about 50 kcal/km for walking) (est.). Each tbsp of sweet chutney adds about 0.5 km of running.

navratri.reason: besan is chickpea (a pulse) flour, and pulses and grains (sooji too) are avoided on the common North and West Indian Navratri vrat rule set; vrat "dhokla" is made from samak rice or rajgira, a different dish

ekadashi.reason: besan is a pulse flour, and grains and pulses are the foods given up on Ekadashi; sooji is wheat

jain.reason: leave out the ginger (fresh root); the rest fits common Jain practice, and "Jain dhokla" is a standard farsan-shop item

ramadan.reason: vegetarian, so there is no halal concern; light, soft and moderately salty, a common iftar farsan in Gujarati homes; for sehri it is lighter than a full meal, so pair it with curd or chai

jain.reason: skip the ginger in the ginger-chilli paste (ginger is a fresh root); everything else (besan, sooji, oil, mustard, sesame, curry leaves, green chilli, lemon) fits common Jain practice

vegan.reason: no dairy, ghee, honey or egg; the batter and tempering use groundnut oil, and eno is sodium bicarbonate, citric acid and sodium carbonate

pescatarian.reason: vegetarian, no meat, fish or egg, so it fits a pescatarian diet

sattvik.reason: no onion or garlic; the flavour comes from ginger, green chilli, lemon, mustard seeds and curry leaves

glutenFree.reason: besan is gluten-free, but the 1 tsp sooji (semolina, wheat) and compounded hing (usually bulked with wheat flour) contain gluten; leave out the sooji and use hing labelled gluten-free or none

dairyFree.reason: no milk, curd or ghee in this recipe (some recipes add curd to the batter; this one does not)

description: A vegetarian, vegan, dairy-free and sattvik (no onion, no garlic) steamed Gujarati gram-flour snack; Jain and gluten-free versions below.

variants.reason: . Main recipe already vegan (oil, no curd or ghee).
